title: Four Abominations in the Temple
sum: In September 592 BC, as the elders of Judah sit in Ezekiel's house in Babylon, a figure of fire lifts him by the hair and carries him, in a vision, to the Temple in Jerusalem. There he is shown four scenes, each worse than the last: an image of jealousy at the north gate, seventy elders burning incense before carvings hidden on a wall, women weeping for Tammuz, and twenty-five men bowing to the sun with their backs to the LORD's house.

The target is the elders' own saying, "The LORD does not see us. The LORD has left the land" (8:12). The vision shows that he sees all of it. The chapter ends with his answer: rage, no compassion, no hearing (8:18). The next chapters show the sentence carried out.
readings: Read as a report of what was done

Some interpreters take the four scenes as a fair picture of worship in the Temple before and after 597 BC: Manasseh's idols had come back under Jehoiakim and Zedekiah (2 Kings 23:37; 24:19), the women's weeping is the kind of devotion Jeremiah describes (Jeremiah 7:18; 44:17-19), and the sun-worship matches what Josiah had to remove (2 Kings 23:5, 11). On this reading the vision shows Ezekiel, a priest's son who knew that Temple, what he already knows or has heard.
Read as a composed indictment

Others see a literary arrangement: Ezekiel gathers every kind of wrong worship into four scenes that move inward to the altar, and each one is introduced by "you will see still more". On this reading the point is not to list what happened in 592, but to say that the whole sanctuary was already defiled. The scenes need not be false to be selected.
Read as vision, not tour

Because the journey is "in visions of God" (8:3; 11:24), the scenes are what the LORD showed, not what a visitor would have seen. That leaves open whether each scene had a counterpart in Jerusalem, and lets readers learn from the chapter's logic: nothing is hidden from him.

views.H: Jerusalem in 592 BC had lost its king and many of its leaders to exile in 597. Those left behind, including the Temple staff, were saying that the exiles had gone far from the LORD and the land was theirs (11:15). Ezekiel's vision gives the opposite verdict: the people at home are the ones driving the LORD from his house. Almost six years later the city fell and the Temple burned (2 Kings 25:8-9).
views.C: Chapters 8-11 read as one unit but not as one piece. Many critical commentators think the vision grew in stages (the four scenes, the killing in chapter 9, the glory's departure in 10-11), with debate over where Ezekiel's own words end and where later editors added. Some also doubt that Ezekiel could have known the details of hidden rooms in Jerusalem, and suggest the scenes are symbolic. Others point out that a priest from the Temple would know it well.
views.J: Jewish tradition remembered this verse in the Sukkot Temple ceremony: those at the east gate turned back toward the Temple and said that their fathers had turned their backs, but "our eyes are toward the LORD" (Mishnah Sukkah 5:4). The rabbis also taught that the Temple's destruction came because of such sins, though they usually name idolatry, bloodshed and immorality together (Yoma 9b).
views.X: Christian readers have used the chapter as a warning about worship inside the community of God: the Temple can be defiled by those who serve in it. Paul tells believers that together they are God's temple and must not be destroyed (1 Corinthians 3:16-17), and Jerome read Tammuz as Adonis and the weeping women as the cult of the pagan year (Commentary on Ezekiel).
views.F: Most readers who look to a future Temple read this chapter as history, not prophecy. Where the chapter bears on the future, it is as a pattern: the glory leaves because the Temple is defiled (chapters 10-11) and comes back only when it is cleansed (43:1-5).

deep.b:
For Ezekiel 8-15 the Plain is translated from the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), verse by verse from a word-for-word rendering. The Dead Sea Scrolls were read through the transcriptions of Martin Abegg, James Bowley and Edward Cook (ETCBC dss). For these eight chapters only one scroll preserves any verse: 4QEzek-a (4Q73), which has fragments of 10:5-11:11, with many words restored by the editors; restored words are never cited here as the scroll's reading. No scroll preserves chapters 8, 9, 12, 13, 14 or 15, and none preserves 11:12 to the end. The Greek was read in Swete's edition, which prints Codex Vaticanus. The critical Greek of Ziegler, Papyrus 967 (the earliest Greek witness to Ezekiel, about the early third century AD) and the later Greek versions of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion are named in notes only as reported by the scholars cited there. The Targum, the Talmud and the medieval Jewish commentators are cited as reported by the editions named in each note.

Spelling differences in the Hebrew (the Ketiv and Qere at 8:6; 9:4-5; 9:11; 12:14 and the spelling of Daniel at 14:14, 20) are not listed as variants unless they change the sense. The Ketiv and Qere at 14:4 do change it and have their own entry. Where a note says "the Greek" it means Swete's printed text of Codex Vaticanus.

The four scenes move inward and upward in holiness. The first is at the north gate of the inner court (8:3-6), the second in a hidden room off the court (8:7-13), the third at the north gate of the Temple (8:14), the fourth between the porch and the altar (8:16), the most sacred ground that anyone but the priests could reach. Each time Ezekiel hears "you will see still more". The movement matches the movement of the glory in the chapters that follow, which leaves from the same inner places toward the east (9:3; 10:4, 18-19; 11:22-23).

echoes: 2 Kings 21:1-9; 2 Kings 23:4-14; 2 Chronicles 33:1-9; Jeremiah 7:16-20; Jeremiah 44:15-19; Deuteronomy 4:15-19; Deuteronomy 17:2-5; Ezekiel 9:9; Ezekiel 10:18-19; Ezekiel 11:22-23; Ezekiel 43:1-5; 1 Corinthians 3:16-17

settings.what: The vision of the Temple: its abominations, the slaughter and the glory's departure
settings.by: The Lord GOD, who shows Ezekiel the vision; a figure of fire leads him (8:2-3) and later the LORD speaks directly
settings.to: Ezekiel first, then the exiles at Tel-abib, to whom he tells it (11:25); the elders of Judah were sitting before him when it began (8:1)
settings.when: The sixth year of Jehoiachin's exile, sixth month, fifth day (about September 592 BC), almost six years before Jerusalem fell
settings.why: To answer the saying "The LORD has left the land" (8:12) and the hope of the exiles that Jerusalem stood safe: the vision shows what the people at home are doing, why the city will be judged, and that the LORD himself is leaving his Temple
settings.readers: For the exiles who read the collected book after 586 BC, these chapters explained why the Temple fell: the LORD had left it first, and not because Babylon's gods were stronger.
views: The scenes mirror what Ezekiel knew of the Temple before 597 BC and what reports from Jerusalem told him.
The four scenes are a literary gathering of every form of false worship, shaped to prove that the Temple was already unclean.

title: The Mark and the Killing
sum: The vision continues. The LORD calls out that the punishments have come. Six men with smashing weapons arrive from the north gate, and with them a seventh in linen with a scribe's case. The glory moves from its place over the cherub to the threshold. The man in linen is sent through the city to mark the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over the abhorrent things done in it. The six follow with orders to kill without pity, young and old, women and children, but not anyone with the mark. The killing begins at the Temple, with the elders.

Ezekiel falls on his face and asks whether the LORD will destroy all the remnant. The answer is the guilt of Israel and Judah: bloodshed, crookedness, and the saying "the LORD has left the land." The man in linen reports his job done. Judgment is real and complete, but it distinguishes: a faithful few are marked and spared.
readings: Read as a vision of Jerusalem's coming fall

The chapter prepares the exiles for news that the city fell and the Temple burned in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:8-9). The six men are the LORD's instruments, as Babylon was in history (Jeremiah 25:9). The mark shows that the fall would not be blind: the righteous who mourned would not be treated as the wicked who did not.
Read as the pattern of final judgment

The mark and the sparing are taken up in Revelation 7 and 9, where God's servants are sealed on the forehead. Read this way, Ezekiel's scene is the first form of a picture that runs through the Bible: the Passover blood (Exodus 12), the mark, the seal.
Read as a problem of justice

Some readers feel the horror of the order: women and children killed. The text itself shares the feeling in Ezekiel's cry in 9:8. The answer it gives is the people's own guilt and their denial that the LORD sees; later in the book it shifts to individual responsibility (chapter 18) and the LORD's own pleasure in life rather than death (18:23, 32).

views.H: In 592 BC Jerusalem still stood, so the slaughter is a prophecy of what came in 586. The Babylonians did kill many in the city and burned the Temple (2 Kings 25:8-9; Jeremiah 52:12-13), while many others were taken to Babylon (2 Kings 25:11).
views.C: Chapter 9 is generally taken as part of the long Temple vision (8-11). Some critical commentators think the sparing of the marked (9:4, 6) was added to an earlier, harsher scene; others find it original. Verses 9-10 repeat the saying quoted in 8:12 and the refrain of 8:18, which ties the chapter to what comes before.
views.J: The Talmud reads the tav as a test of justice: if the righteous were marked, why were some of them struck with the wicked? It answers that those who could have protested and did not were not free of blame (Shabbat 55a). Rashi reads the sign as protection for the righteous (on 9:4), and Jewish tradition takes the man in linen to be Gabriel (Shabbat 55a).
views.X: Early Christian writers read the tav as a sign of the cross: Origen, Tertullian and Jerome are among those who do (Jerome, Commentary on Ezekiel). Revelation 7:3 and 9:4 later speak of a seal on the foreheads of God's servants.
views.F: Readers who expect a future tribulation treat the chapter as one pattern for the end: a believing remnant is marked and kept, while judgment falls on a defiled religious center. Revelation 7:3 and 9:4 use the same picture, and futurist writers often cite Ezekiel 9 beside those chapters.

deep.h: The sparing mark and who gets it
deep.b:
The marked are "the people who sigh and groan over all the abhorrent things done in it" (9:4). They are not described as sinless, only as sorrowing and unwilling to take part. This is a different standard from the one in chapter 14, where Noah, Daniel and Job could save only themselves, and from chapter 18, where each person lives or dies by his own way. Chapter 9 is about a city, and the saving mark falls on individuals within it.

The scene also changes how readers hear the later chapters. The people who keep saying "the LORD does not see" are told the opposite: a scribe has been writing down who mourned.

echoes: Exodus 12:7, 13, 23; Revelation 7:2-4; Revelation 9:4; Revelation 14:1; 1 Peter 4:17; Jeremiah 25:29; Amos 7:1-6; Daniel 10:5; Genesis 18:23-25; Ezekiel 8:12; Ezekiel 10:4; Ezekiel 14:12-20

settings.what: The six executioners and the man with the writing case
settings.by: The LORD, speaking from the glory to the man in linen and the six, and then to Ezekiel (9:9-10)
settings.to: The six heavenly figures and the man in linen inside the vision; Ezekiel hears it, and later tells the exiles (11:25)
settings.when: Part of the same vision as chapter 8 (September 592 BC), almost six years before the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC
settings.why: To show the exiles that the coming destruction is the LORD's own act, that it will begin at the Temple, and that those who grieve over the city's sins will be marked and spared
settings.readers: After 586 BC the exiles who read this saw in it an explanation of the fall: the city was not defeated because the LORD was blind to it, but because he had acted. It also gave the grieving survivors a reason to believe they had been known.

title: The Glory Leaves the Threshold
sum: The man in linen is told to take burning coals from between the cherubim, under the throne, and scatter them over the city. The cherubim, with their wheels full of eyes, stand at the south side of the house, and the cloud fills the court. The glory of the LORD rises from the cherub to the threshold; the sound of the wings can be heard in the outer court.

Ezekiel describes the cherubim and their wheels again and says that these are the living creatures he saw at the Kebar canal. Then the glory goes out from the threshold, mounts the cherubim, and stops at the east gate. The throne of the Holy of Holies is moving out of the Temple. The chapter is the book's turning point: the glory that Israel thought would guard the city is leaving it.
readings: Read as the departure of the LORD

On the traditional reading the LORD's own presence withdraws from the Temple in stages. The people in Jerusalem said the LORD had left the land (8:12); in fact he leaves only now, and he leaves because of what they did. His going is the cause of the city's fall, not its result.
Read as a recasting of chapter 1

Many critics see chapter 10 as a re-reading of chapter 1 in Temple language: the creatures are called cherubim, the wheels get the extra name galgal, and the throne moves from the Kebar canal to the Temple. On this view 10:9-17, which repeats 1:15-21, was added to tie the two visions together.
Read as a mobile throne

The cherubim and wheels make a movable throne, a chariot. The point of the vision is that God is not tied to a place: his throne can go to Babylon and back. The same picture that comforts the exiles in chapter 1 judges the city here.

views.H: The departure of the glory happens in a vision in 592 BC. The Temple was burned in 586 BC, so the stages of departure in 9:3, 10:4, 10:18-19 and 11:22-23 are a four-year warning. Chronicles and Kings say nothing about the glory leaving; they say only that the Temple was burned (2 Kings 25:9; 2 Chronicles 36:19).
views.C: Chapter 10 is the most debated in the Temple vision. It repeats words from chapter 1 almost word for word (10:9-17 with 1:15-21), adds the name galgal and the fire-taking scene, and ends by identifying the creatures as cherubim. Most critical commentators think the chapter has been shaped and expanded; Block and Greenberg read it as Ezekiel's own composition.
views.J: The Talmud counts ten journeys of the Presence from the Temple to heaven, passing the cherub, the threshold, the city and the mountain east of it (Rosh Hashanah 31a). Hagigah 13b explains the change from "ox" to "cherub" in 10:14 as Ezekiel's prayer that the golden calf not be recalled against Israel. Later Jewish mystics built their study of the chariot on Ezekiel's vision.
views.X: Christian readers saw in the Temple's forsaken house a pattern for what Jesus said of the Temple in Matthew 23:38. The cherubim and four faces were read by many fathers as signs of the four Gospels (Irenaeus on chapter 1).
views.F: Readers who expect a future Temple read the departure and return of the glory (10:18-19; 43:1-5) as a pattern: the LORD leaves because of defilement and returns to a cleansed house. Some also connect the cherubim of this chapter with those in Revelation 4:6-8.

deep.b: Chapter 1 never calls the winged creatures "cherubim"; chapter 10 says they are (10:15, 20). The cherubim in the Bible are guardians: at Eden's gate (Genesis 3:24), on the Ark's lid (Exodus 25:18-22), carved on the Temple walls and doors (1 Kings 6:23-35), and as a mount for the LORD (Psalm 18:10). In Ezekiel they are also the bearers of the throne. The Temple cherubim and the creatures at the Kebar are the same beings; what Ezekiel saw in Babylon is what stands in the Holy of Holies.

echoes: Ezekiel 1:4-28; Ezekiel 9:3; Ezekiel 11:22-23; Ezekiel 43:1-5; Isaiah 6:1-7; Exodus 25:18-22; 1 Kings 6:23-35; 1 Kings 8:10-11; Psalm 18:10; Revelation 4:6-8; Revelation 8:5; Matthew 23:38

settings.what: The coals from the cherubim and the departure of the glory
settings.by: The LORD, speaking to the man in linen (10:2, 6); Ezekiel describes what he sees
settings.to: The man in linen inside the vision; Ezekiel, and through him the exiles at Tel-abib to whom he tells it (11:25)
settings.when: The same vision as chapters 8 and 9 (September 592 BC), almost six years before the Temple was burned
settings.why: To show that the destruction begins with the LORD's own act and that the glory has left before the Babylonians came, so that the exiles would not think the LORD had been defeated
settings.readers: The exiles who read the book after 586 BC saw that the Temple fell because its God had already left, and that the same God could be with them in Babylon, because his throne moved.

title: The Pot and the Little Sanctuary
sum: The vision ends where it began, with Ezekiel at the Temple's east gate. There he sees twenty-five men, two named, who plan harm in the city. They boast that Jerusalem is a pot and they are the meat, safe inside. Ezekiel prophesies: the slain are the meat, and the leaders will be taken out and judged at the border. While he speaks, Pelatiah dies, and Ezekiel falls down and cries out for the remnant.

The LORD answers with hope. The people in Jerusalem tell the exiles that they are far from the LORD and that the land is now theirs. But the LORD has become a little sanctuary for the exiles, will gather them, give them one heart and a new spirit, and make them his people again. Then the cherubim lift their wings, the glory rises from the city and stops on the mountain east of it, and the vision is over. Ezekiel tells the exiles all he saw.
readings: Read as judgment and promise

The chapter is two halves: judgment on the officials who feel safe (11:1-13), and a promise to the exiles whom they scorned (11:14-21). Jerusalem's leaders say the exiles are far from the LORD; the LORD says he is with the exiles and will bring them back.
Read as the end of the Temple's era

The glory goes up, and its last stop is the mountain east of the city. The LORD has left the Temple, but the exiles are not left alone, since he is a sanctuary for them. Later Jews and Christians took this as the beginning of worship without the Temple.
Read as the start of the new covenant hope

The new heart, new spirit and covenant formula of 11:19-20 are the first statement of a promise that chapter 36 develops fully and that Jeremiah 31:31-34 pairs with a new covenant. Christian readers see it fulfilled by the Spirit; Jewish readers see it as still being fulfilled.

views.H: The officials of 11:1 are the men who led Jerusalem in the years after 597 BC, under Zedekiah. The saying that Jerusalem is a pot recalls the confidence that kept Zedekiah from surrendering (Jeremiah 38:17-23). In 586 BC many leaders were taken to Riblah and killed (2 Kings 25:18-21), which some readers connect with the promise to judge them "at the border of Israel" (11:10-11).
views.C: Chapter 11 is often read in two layers. The first, 11:1-13, belongs with the Temple vision; the second, 11:14-21, a word of hope addressed to the exiles, may have been added to the vision or may be Ezekiel's own response to it. Some critics think the promise of a new heart (11:19-20) is too close to chapter 36 to be early. Others, such as Greenberg and Block, treat it as Ezekiel's.
views.J: The Talmud reads the "little sanctuary" as the synagogues and houses of study in Babylon (Megillah 29a), and the exile as a place where the Presence went with the people. The same passage teaches that the Presence went into exile with Israel. The Presence's waiting on the Mount of Olives for three and a half years is told in Rosh Hashanah 31a.
views.X: Christian readers connected the glory's stop on the Mount of Olives with Jesus' ascension from the same mountain (Acts 1:9-12). The new heart and new spirit of 11:19 were read as the gift of the Spirit in baptism and conversion (compare Ezekiel 36:25-27).
views.F: For readers who look to a future for Israel, 11:17-20 is part of the promise of a return and a spiritual renewal, along with chapters 36-37. The glory that stops on the Mount of Olives and returns by the east gate (43:1-5) is linked by many to Zechariah 14:4.

deep.b: Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah are the only people named in the vision besides Jaazaniah son of Shaphan (8:11). Nothing else is known of them. The text does not say what office they held, only that they are "officials of the people" and that one of them dies as Ezekiel speaks. The death is told inside the vision, in the same way that all the vision's events are told.

echoes: Ezekiel 8:12; Ezekiel 9:8; Ezekiel 10:19; Ezekiel 24:3-14; Ezekiel 36:24-28; Ezekiel 37:26-28; Ezekiel 43:1-5; Jeremiah 1:13; Jeremiah 7:4; Jeremiah 24; Jeremiah 29:5; Jeremiah 31:33; Jeremiah 32:39; Zechariah 14:4; Acts 1:9-12

settings.what: The oracle against the twenty-five officials
settings.by: The Spirit of the LORD, who tells Ezekiel what to say (11:5)
settings.to: Jaazaniah, Pelatiah and the other officials at the east gate, inside the vision; Ezekiel later tells the exiles (11:25)
settings.when: Within the Temple vision of September 592 BC, almost six years before the fall
settings.why: To break the confidence of Jerusalem's leaders, who thought the city's walls would protect them, and to show the exiles that their leaders at home were not safe
settings.readers: After 586 BC, readers saw in 11:1-13 a record of why Zedekiah's government failed.

settings.what: The word to the exiles: a little sanctuary and a new heart
settings.to: The exiles, called Ezekiel's "brothers" and "the whole house of Israel" (11:15), who had been told by the people of Jerusalem that they were far from the LORD
settings.when: After the vision's tour and Pelatiah's death, before the glory leaves (11:22-23)
settings.why: To answer the claim in Jerusalem that the exiles had lost both the LORD and the land, and to promise the exiles his presence, a return and a renewed heart
settings.readers: For the exiles and for later generations who lived away from the land and the Temple, this was the first promise that the LORD would be present in exile and would one day gather them.
views: The little sanctuary as a place
The exiles' meeting places, the synagogues and houses of study (Megillah 29a), are the sanctuary.
The little sanctuary as God himself
The LORD himself is their sanctuary, as he is to those who trust him in Psalm 90:1 and 91:9.

title: Packing for Exile
sum: Ezekiel is told that the people around him have eyes and ears but do not see or hear. So he acts out an exile in daylight: he packs a bundle, carries it out through a hole dug in his house wall at dusk, with his face covered. When the people ask what he is doing, he explains: the leader in Jerusalem will do this. He will slip out through the wall at night, covering his face, be caught in the LORD's net, and be taken to Babylon, where he will die without seeing it. His helpers will be scattered.

Three more messages follow: Ezekiel is to eat and drink with shaking, as a sign of the fear that is coming to the land; the proverb "The days drag on, and every vision fails" will be ended; and the LORD will do what he says in the days of this rebellious house, with no more delay.
readings: Read as a prediction fulfilled

On the traditional reading the sign act is a precise prediction of Zedekiah's flight and blinding in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:4-7). Ezekiel says Zedekiah will be brought to Babylon but will not see it, and 2 Kings 25:7 and Jeremiah 52:11 tell of a king blinded at Riblah and taken to Babylon, where he died.
Read as street theater

Ezekiel is a performer whose acts are meant to make people ask, and the chapter says outright that they did (12:9). The sign is not a code to decode but a scene to see, and what he wants is for the people to ask, so that he can answer.
Read as a word against false hope

The second half of the chapter takes aim at the people's way of dismissing prophecy: it will come later, it will come to others, or it will not come at all. The chapter ends by saying there will be no more delay (12:25, 28).

views.H: Ezekiel's sign is acted in about 592 BC, during the reign of Zedekiah (597-586). The Babylonians took Zedekiah to Riblah, and he was blinded after his sons were killed (2 Kings 25:7; Jeremiah 52:10-11). Many readers count this among the book's closest matches with later events, though the critical view below asks whether the account was shaped by them. The chapter gives the exiles almost six years' warning.
views.C: Some critical commentators think the prediction in 12:12-13 has been shaped by what happened in 586, since it matches the fall so closely. Others point out that the details are not given in advance in Ezekiel (he does not say "blinded"), and that the prediction would have been plausible to anyone who knew the usual fate of captured kings. The omission of 12:26-28 from Papyrus 967 is also discussed, as one case of the shorter Greek text.
views.J: Jewish tradition took the leader as Zedekiah and read the account as a double prophecy that came true together with Jeremiah's. Josephus, a first-century Jewish historian, tells how Zedekiah, hearing that Jeremiah said he would see Babylon and Ezekiel that he would not, believed neither; both came true when he was blinded and taken there (Jewish Antiquities 10.6.3, §§106-107; the blinding is told in 10.7.2, §§141-142).
views.X: Christian writers read the sign as a prophecy of the end of the Temple state and of the fall of Jerusalem, and the saying "the days drag on" as the scoffers' voice in 2 Peter 3:3-4. The idea that prophecy cannot be delayed is taken up in Hebrews 10:37 (quoting Habakkuk 2:3).
views.F: Readers who look to a future end see in the proverb "the days drag on" a pattern for every generation that says the promised end is too far away to matter. They cite 2 Peter 3 as the Christian form of this answer.

deep.b: The verse that Zedekiah "will not see" Babylon has a reputation as a riddle, and it is easy to see why: Zedekiah was blinded and then taken to Babylon, so he arrived but did not see it. The Hebrew says only that he will not see the land with his eye (12:12), and the Greek says the same. Whether Ezekiel knew of the blinding when he spoke, or the words were given their present form after it, cannot be said from the text. It is clear that the exiles who first read the book after 586 found the match exact.

echoes: 2 Kings 25:4-7; Jeremiah 34:3; Jeremiah 39:4-7; Jeremiah 52:7-11; Isaiah 6:9-10; Jeremiah 5:21; Deuteronomy 29:4; Isaiah 5:19; Jeremiah 17:15; Habakkuk 2:3; 2 Peter 3:3-9; Hebrews 10:37; Ezekiel 4:1-5:4; Ezekiel 17:20

settings.what: The sign of the baggage and its meaning
settings.by: Ezekiel, acting out the LORD's command; the LORD explains it the next morning (12:8-16)
settings.to: The exiles at Tel-abib, who watch and ask "What are you doing?" (12:9); the message is about the leader (Zedekiah) and the people left in Jerusalem
settings.when: Not dated; it follows the vision of September 592 BC (chapters 8-11) and comes before 20:1 (591 BC), almost six years before Jerusalem fell
settings.why: To show the exiles, who thought they would soon go home, that more people were still to go into exile and that their leader would not escape; to break the hope that Jerusalem would stand
settings.readers: After 586 BC readers saw Zedekiah's flight and blinding in this chapter and understood that the LORD had told them.
views: Nearly all interpreters, ancient and modern, take the nasi as King Zedekiah.
Some scholars think the acts were told as a literary form and not literally performed in front of the exiles.

settings.what: The sign of eating with trembling
settings.to: "The people of the land" (12:19): the exiles in Babylon, about those who remained in Jerusalem
settings.when: Not dated; placed after the sign of the baggage
settings.why: To make the coming siege and desolation felt: those who still live in Jerusalem will eat their bread in fear because of the violence in the land
settings.readers: For later readers the sign was a record of how the siege felt to those inside, as Lamentations 5:9-10 tells it.

settings.what: The two answers to the proverb about delayed vision
settings.to: The house of Israel, who say the vision is for the distant future (12:22, 27)
settings.when: Not dated; the exiles' waiting after 597 BC, before the siege began in 588
settings.why: To end the saying that prophecy always lies in the future and will not touch the present, so that people stop using delay as an excuse for ignoring warnings
settings.readers: For readers after 586 BC, the saying was proved wrong; for readers in every later age, the chapter is a warning about the habit of saying that the warning is for someone else or for some other time.

title: Whitewash on a Weak Wall
sum: Ezekiel is told to speak against the prophets of Israel who prophesy out of their own hearts. They have seen nothing and still say, "The LORD declares." They are like foxes in ruins: they did not repair the breaches or build a wall for the day of battle. They have led the people astray by saying "Peace!" when there is no peace, and have plastered a weak wall with whitewash. The LORD will send a flood, hail and storm, and the wall will fall.

Then Ezekiel turns to women who prophesy out of their own hearts. They tie bands on people's wrists and spread veils over their heads to hunt lives, for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread. They kill those who should not die and keep alive those who should not live. They have saddened the righteous and strengthened the wicked. The LORD will tear off their bands and veils and free his people.
readings: Read as a test of prophets

The chapter gives marks of a false prophet: the LORD did not send him, he speaks out of his own heart, he says "peace" when there is none, he does not repair breaches, and he profits. The test is the one in Deuteronomy 18:20-22, applied to the exiles' own day.
Read as political criticism

Some scholars read the wall as Judah's resistance to Babylon with Egypt's help (17:15) and the whitewash as the prophets' reassurance. On this reading chapter 13 addresses the same policy as chapters 12 and 17.
Read as a charge of selling words

The women who sell their services for barley and bread (13:19) and the prophets who live among ruins point to people who profit from the people's fear. The chapter protects the vulnerable by naming those who sell them false hope.

views.H: In 592-588 BC, between the deportation of 597 and the siege of Jerusalem, many prophets told both the exiles and those in Jerusalem that the Babylonian yoke would soon be broken (Jeremiah 28:1-4; 29:8-9). The fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC proved them wrong, and the wall of 13:12 fell as Ezekiel had said.
views.C: Chapter 13 is closely tied to Jeremiah 23 and 28-29 in theme, and a number of scholars see a shared tradition of prophetic criticism of prophets. The women's section (13:17-23) is the hardest to interpret, because the practices named have no clear parallel in the Hebrew Bible. Some commentators think the second half is a separate oracle that was attached to the first.
views.J: Jewish law makes a prophet who speaks what he was not told, or speaks in the name of an idol, a capital offender (Deuteronomy 18:20; Mishnah Sanhedrin 11:5). Ezekiel 13 is read with Jeremiah 28 (Hananiah) as the biblical case of how the test of fulfillment works.
views.X: The New Testament uses the chapter's images twice: Paul calls the high priest Ananias a "whitewashed wall" (Acts 23:3), and Jesus calls the Pharisees "whitewashed tombs" (Matthew 23:27). The parable of the house on sand (Matthew 7:24-27) uses the same rain, flood and wind.
views.F: Readers who look to the end of the age cite the warnings about false prophets in the last days (Matthew 24:11, 24; 2 Peter 2:1) as the continuing form of this chapter: a leading sign is that many say "peace" when there is no peace (1 Thessalonians 5:3).

deep.b: The practices of 13:17-23 are hard to reconstruct. The bands (kesatot) and veils (mispachot) are rare words, and their uses are unknown: no other Hebrew text describes them. The key phrase, "hunt lives", appears twice. Scholars have understood it as a form of magic that claimed power over life and death, and have compared knot-magic and cloth rituals in Mesopotamia. Others think the women were professional diviners or healers who claimed to know who would live or die, and sold favorable words. What the text itself makes clear is the moral charge: they lied to people who trusted them, for pay, and so strengthened the wicked and discouraged the righteous.

echoes: Jeremiah 6:14; Jeremiah 8:11; Jeremiah 23:9-40; Jeremiah 28; Jeremiah 29:8-9; Deuteronomy 18:20-22; Micah 3:5-11; Isaiah 28:15-17; Matthew 7:24-27; Matthew 23:27; Acts 23:3; Ezekiel 22:28; Ezekiel 22:30

settings.what: The oracle against the prophets who say "peace"
settings.by: The LORD, through Ezekiel, who is told to prophesy against them
settings.to: The prophets of Israel and, as a warning, the exiles who listen to them; Ezekiel speaks to the prophets, but his hearers are the exiles in Babylon
settings.when: Not dated; in the period after the vision of September 592 BC and before the siege began in 588 BC
settings.why: To teach the exiles not to trust prophets who promise peace, and to tell the prophets that their word will fall like a wall in a storm
settings.readers: After 586 BC, readers could see that the wall had fallen and that the prophets of peace had been wrong, and took this as a test for later prophets.
views: Ezekiel addresses prophets in the city, who prophesy peace for it (13:16), and his words reach them through the exiles and through letters like Jeremiah 29.
Ezekiel addresses prophets who were with him in Babylon, as in Jeremiah 29:8-9, 21-23, who said the exile would be short.

settings.what: The oracle against the women who prophesy and tie bands
settings.to: The women who prophesied out of their own hearts, and the exiles who might come to them
settings.when: Not dated; the same period as 13:1-16
settings.why: To end the practice of buying lives and deaths for a few scraps of food, and to show that the LORD will free the people from those who trapped them
settings.readers: For later readers it showed that the LORD protects the powerless from those who prey on their fear.

title: Idols in the Heart; Noah, Daniel and Job
sum: Elders of the exiles come to Ezekiel's house to ask a word from the LORD. The LORD tells Ezekiel that these men have idols in their hearts and a stumbling block of guilt before their faces, and that he will answer anyone like that himself, "in keeping with his many idols". The call is to turn back. A prophet who is deceived has been deceived by the LORD, and prophet and inquirer will bear the same guilt.

Then the LORD gives a rule in four cases. If a land sins and he sends famine, wild animals, a sword or a plague, even Noah, Daniel and Job would save only themselves, not their sons or daughters. How much worse when all four come on Jerusalem. Yet some survivors will be led out to the exiles, and their conduct will show that the LORD did nothing without cause.
readings: Read as a rule about idols and inquiry

The first half teaches that asking God is not enough when the heart is divided. The elders sit politely before the prophet, but their hearts are with other things, and the LORD answers according to what is in the heart.
Read as a rule about righteousness

The second half sets a limit on borrowed righteousness. Great saints would save themselves, but not their children. It prepares the argument of chapter 18, where each person lives or dies for himself.
Read as a defense of God's justice
The closing verses answer the question the exiles would ask on hearing of Jerusalem's fall: was it just? The survivors will arrive and the exiles will see for themselves why.

views.H: The elders' visit comes in the years between the first deportation (597) and the siege (588). The four judgments are those that Jerusalem actually met in the siege of 588-586: famine (Lamentations 4:9-10), sword, plague and, in the depopulated land, wild animals (compare Lamentations 5:18). The survivors are the refugees who reached Babylon after 586 (33:21).
views.C: Chapter 14 is a collection of three units: 14:1-11 on inquiry and idols, 14:12-20 on the four judgments, and 14:21-23 on the survivors. Many scholars see 14:21-23 as a later addition (it fits the aftermath of 586, and the "comfort" they bring is of a different kind). The mention of Daniel beside Noah and Job is much discussed because the book of Daniel puts him in Babylon in 605 BC, while the spelling and the order suggest an ancient hero (compare 28:3).
views.J: Jewish interpreters have long asked whether this Daniel is the exile of the book of Daniel, who was a young man in Babylon when Ezekiel spoke. On 14:9 Rashi reads "I enticed" as "I opened a doorway for him to whatever he wishes", a judgment in which the prophet is let go his own way; Radak compares the case of Ahab (1 Kings 22) (Rashi and Radak on Ezekiel 14:9).
views.X: Jerome took Daniel as the exile prophet. Calvin's saying that the human mind is a factory of idols (Institutes 1.11.8) is often applied to 14:3, a charge against the heart. Chapter 14 is often quoted in the debate over whether one person's righteousness can help another.
views.F: Readers who look to the end of the age read the four judgments as the pattern for the four horsemen of Revelation 6:8, and the survivors who comfort the exiles as the remnant who come through the final tribulation.

deep.h: The rule is not about prayer
deep.b: Some readers have taken 14:14-20 as a statement that intercession is useless. That reading overlooks what the passage does with the three men. Noah, Job and Daniel are known in their stories for rescuing or praying for others; Ezekiel chooses them for exactly that reason. His claim is about a land whose guilt is complete: when God has decided, no one's righteousness turns the judgment, not even theirs. In the same period Ezekiel himself prays for the remnant (9:8; 11:13), and Jeremiah is told not to pray for the people (Jeremiah 7:16; 15:1). The rule is a statement about the limit of this generation's case, not about the use of prayer in general.

echoes: Genesis 6-9; Genesis 18:23-32; Job 1-2; Job 42:7-9; Daniel 1-2; Leviticus 26:21-26; Deuteronomy 13:1-5; 1 Kings 22:19-23; Jeremiah 5:31; Jeremiah 15:1-4; Revelation 6:8; Romans 1:24-28; 2 Thessalonians 2:11; Ezekiel 18:20; Ezekiel 28:3

settings.what: Elders who inquire with idols in their hearts
settings.by: The LORD, to Ezekiel, who is to tell the elders
settings.to: The elders of Israel who came and sat before Ezekiel, and through them the whole house of Israel (14:5-6)
settings.when: Not dated; between the vision of 592 BC and the dated word of 20:1 (591 BC)
settings.why: To stop the exiles from treating Ezekiel as a source of comfort while keeping their idols, and to tell them that a prophet who tells them what they want is a sign of the LORD's judgment
settings.readers: After 586 BC the chapter explained why the exiles' hopes of a quick return were false: the elders who inquired were the ones who could not repent.

settings.what: The four judgments and the three righteous men
settings.to: The exiles, who hoped that righteous people in Jerusalem (or their own prayers) would save the city
settings.when: Not dated; the same period as 14:1-11
settings.why: To end the hope that Jerusalem could be spared because a few righteous people lived in it, or because they would pray
settings.readers: Later readers saw a limit on one person's merit that Ezekiel 18 develops.
views: The passage describes a land whose guilt is complete and does not teach anything about prayer in general.
The passage teaches that no one's righteousness can be credited to another.

settings.what: The survivors who comfort the exiles
settings.when: Not dated; its content looks ahead to the survivors of 586 BC
settings.why: To tell the exiles that when the survivors arrive, their ways will show that the judgment was just, and they will be comforted
settings.readers: For readers after 586 BC, the verses explained how the survivors confirmed what Ezekiel had said.

traditions.q: Can the righteous save others by their righteousness or their prayers? (Ezekiel 14:14, 20) The verses describe a land whose guilt is complete; whether they limit what the righteous can do for others in general is where churches differ.
views: The saints in heaven are united with Christ and pray for the Church, and Catholics ask for their prayers; the merits of the saints are gifts of Christ shared in the communion of saints (Catechism 956, 1477, 2683).
The saints in heaven pray for the living and the departed, and the Orthodox ask for their prayers; the Confession of Dositheus (1672) calls the saints intercessors (Decree 8).

The saints are to be remembered as examples of faith, and Christ alone is the mediator; Scripture does not command invoking the saints (Augsburg Confession 21). The Apology grants that the saints in heaven may pray for the Church in general, but not that they must be called on.
Religious worship, prayer included, is to be given to God alone, not to angels, saints or any other creature (Westminster Confession 21.2).
Article 22 rejects the medieval doctrine of invoking saints as having no warrant in Scripture (Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 22).

traditions.q: Does God cause a prophet to be deceived, or only permit it? (Ezekiel 14:9) The real difference: whether God's rule over sin is "permission" or something more.
views: God's providence reaches even the sins of angels and men, and "not by a bare permission" but with a wise and powerful governing of them, though the sinfulness comes only from the creature and not from God (Westminster Confession 5.4); as a righteous judge he may blind and harden the wicked for earlier sins (5.6). Calvin treats God's use of lying spirits, as with Ahab, as God's ordering of the wicked to his ends while he stays clean of their guilt (Institutes 1.18).

God's foreknowledge is not the cause of evil, which comes from the devil and the wicked human will; hardening and blinding are God's judgment on those who have already resisted (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration 11).
God is in no way, directly or indirectly, the cause of moral evil; he permits it, respecting the freedom of creatures, and mysteriously brings good from it (Catechism 311).

title: The Useless Vine
sum: Ezekiel is asked a plain question: what is the wood of the vine good for, compared with any other tree in the forest? The answer is nothing. It makes no tool, not even a peg to hang a vessel on. It is given to the fire for fuel, and a vine burned at both ends and charred in the middle is good for even less.

The LORD explains: the people living in Jerusalem are that wood. They have come out of the fire once, and the fire will consume them. The land will become a desolation because they acted unfaithfully. The chapter is short, and the next, longer chapters of the book take up the picture of Jerusalem's history.
readings: Read as a reversal of the vine image
Israel the vine is a proud image. Here the LORD takes it away: a vine is worth only its fruit, and without fruit is the least useful of trees.
Read as a message to Jerusalem's survivors
The parable answers the people left in Jerusalem after 597 BC, who thought that surviving the first fire showed God's favor.
Read as a short parable in a series
Chapters 15, 16 and 17 give three pictures of Jerusalem and the royal house: the useless vine, the unfaithful wife, the cedar and the eagles. Each deepens the one before.

views.H: The oracle belongs to the years between 597 and 588 BC. Jerusalem still stood, and some in the city thought that the LORD had kept it from the full disaster. The fall in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:8-9) is the burning of what was already charred.
views.C: Chapter 15 is one of the shortest oracles in the book and is often counted a distinct unit: a proverb-like question (15:2-5) and its application (15:6-8). Some critics think the application was added later, but the vine image is one that Ezekiel uses elsewhere (17:5-10; 19:10-14).
views.J: Jewish readers take the vine as Israel, the LORD's own vine (Isaiah 5:7; Psalm 80:8-16), and the chapter as a hard word for the generation of the fall: the privilege of the image is turned into a charge.
views.X: Christian readers connect the chapter with Jesus' words in John 15:1-6, where the branch that does not bear fruit is gathered and burned. The two passages are often read together, though John's vine is Christ and his followers, not Jerusalem.
views.F: For readers who look to the end, the chapter is part of Ezekiel's long argument that Jerusalem could not be saved by its past; the restoration of chapters 36-37 begins only after this has been accepted.

deep.h: A parable that asks a question
deep.b: The vine passage is built as a series of questions to which the answer is obviously no. Ezekiel does not call it a mashal as he does the riddle of chapter 17, but it works as one. The exiles are asked to say what a vine branch is good for, and once they have said "nothing", the LORD applies it to Jerusalem. The method is the one Nathan used with David (2 Samuel 12:1-7): get the hearers to agree to the principle first.

echoes: Isaiah 5:1-7; Psalm 80:8-16; Jeremiah 2:21; Hosea 10:1; John 15:1-6; Ezekiel 17:5-10; Ezekiel 19:10-14; Amos 4:11; 2 Kings 24:10-16; 2 Kings 25:8-9

settings.what: The parable of the useless vine
settings.to: The exiles at Tel-abib, about the people living in Jerusalem
settings.why: To break the confidence of those who thought that surviving the first fall made Jerusalem safe, and to show the exiles that the city has no claim to be saved
settings.readers: After 586 BC readers saw in the vine the fall that had followed: the fire that came out of the first burning consumed the rest.
